Finding.description:
One finding, and the merge-request thread that carries it.

A finding outlives the review that produced it: when a later commit fixes the problem, mrr resolves the thread the earlier review opened rather than posting "this is now fixed" as a new comment.

agentRole.description: The concern this came from — security, tests, performance — as the reviewer named it. Self-reported in one pass, not a separate agent. Null when it did not say, and on every human finding.

approvedBy.description: Forge username of the human who resolved the thread, when the state is APPROVED. Null for OPEN and for ADDRESSED.

origin.description: Who filed it. Null on findings from before origins existed, which were all AGENT.

resolvedAt.description: When it stopped standing — a later commit addressed it, or a human resolved the thread.

severity.description: How bad it is, as judged by the reviewer.

state.description:
OPEN — still standing as of the most recent review.
ADDRESSED — a later commit fixed it; mrr resolved the thread.
APPROVED — a human resolved the thread on the forge, accepting the finding as it stands. mrr records who and keeps the thread closed.
WONT_FIX — a human decided it is real and is not being fixed. The record says who accepted the risk.
DUPLICATE — a human closed it as another finding's twin.
PENDING — the reviewer drafted it and it has not reached the forge, because this project holds findings for a human to release. It still counts against the merge gate: nobody has decided it is wrong, only that nobody has looked yet.
DISCARDED — somebody read a pending finding before it was posted and decided it was not worth raising. Deliberately not WONT_FIX, where the problem is real and the risk was accepted on the record.

There is no DISPUTED state on purpose. A contested finding stays OPEN and keeps counting against the merge gate; the disagreement is a `DISPUTED` event on it. A sixth state would be either a veto anybody could hold indefinitely, or a green merge request with a live disagreement under it.

ADDRESSED — a commit fixed it, or a reply convinced the model it was settled.

REOPENED — it came back.
WONT_FIX, DUPLICATE — a human triaged it.
RELEASED — a human let a held finding through to the forge.
DISCARDED — a human dropped a held finding before it was ever posted.
DISPUTED — somebody contested it. The finding stays OPEN and keeps counting against the merge gate; this records the disagreement, it does not resolve it.
COMMENTED — something was said about it that changed no state.

MergeRequestInfo.description:
The merge request as GitLab described it when this review ran.

A snapshot, not a live view: retitle the MR and push again and you get a second review carrying the new title, with the first left untouched. That history is the point — it is what lets you ask why a review said what it said.

Note the three different people. `author` owns the MR. `actor` triggered this particular delivery. `commitAuthor` wrote the head commit. On a rebase or a cherry-pick these are routinely three different names.

agentTools.description:
Tool names the reviewer may call: `read_file`, `symbol_at`, `find_references`, `co_changed`, `search_memory`, `read_memory`, `write_memory`. Empty means no tools are advertised. The MR card is always written from the verdict, tools or not.

`symbol_at`, `find_references` and `co_changed` read the repository. Enabling any of them makes mrr keep a local mirror of this project under MRR_REPO_ROOT; a project that enables none never gets one. No extra token scope is required — the read access that already backs `read_file` authorises the clone. `symbol_at` also runs before the model is asked anything, expanding every hunk to its enclosing definition, which is why it is worth enabling even on a single-turn review.

token.description:
An mrr API token, as `Authorization: Bearer mrr_…`. `X-API-Key: mrr_…` is accepted as an alternative and is what the MCP endpoint uses.

Tokens are minted by an **admin** token via `POST /api/tokens`. The very first one is printed to the console on first boot and written to `/data/root-token.txt`; it is never recoverable afterwards, because only its SHA-256 hash is stored.

info.description:
AI code review for GitLab merge requests.

A merge request is opened or pushed to, GitLab calls the webhook, mrr pulls the diff, sends it to a model with that project's review instructions, and posts the review back to the MR as a resolvable discussion thread. Every payload, prompt, trace, and response is kept.

## Authentication

Every endpoint under `/api` needs an API token. `/webhooks/gitlab/{projectId}` does **not** — GitLab cannot hold an mrr token, so it authenticates with the per-project secret in `X-Gitlab-Token` instead. `/health` is open.

## Authorization

Three rules govern the whole API:

1. Only an `ADMIN` token can create users or mint tokens. A `USER` token may list    and revoke its own tokens and nothing else.
2. Projects are owned. A `USER` sees and edits only its own; an `ADMIN` sees all.
3. Asking for a project you do not own returns **404, not 403** — a 403 would    confirm that the id exists.

## Reviews are asynchronous

Anything that calls a model returns `202 Accepted` with a `Location` header to poll. A review moves `PENDING → PROCESSING → READY | FAILED`; `READY` and `FAILED` are terminal, so stop polling when you see one.

Reviews are keyed on `(project, mr_iid, head_sha)`. A redelivered webhook, or an `update` event that changed only a label, returns the review that already exists rather than spending tokens on a duplicate. A new push is a new head SHA and so a new review.

## Secrets

GitLab tokens, model keys, and webhook secrets are write-only. They are accepted on create and update, and always masked on read (`****ab12`). The webhook secret is returned exactly once, in the response to `POST /api/projects`.

get.description:
The operator token is the identity a person writes under when they act through mrr — merging, commenting, and filing a finding of their own. Without one those are unavailable.

Two things are checked live: that the forge accepts the token, and who it belongs to. The second is the one that matters — an operator token resolving to the same account as the review bot would put your findings under the agent's name. Whether the token may *write* is not checked, because the only way to test that is to comment on one of your merge requests; that row says so rather than guessing.

post.description:
A finding you raise yourself, not the reviewer's. Same object, same thread, and it counts against the merge gate the same way — the difference is that a later review may not close it. It can say the code looks fixed; you close it by resolving the thread.

Posted with `gitlabOperatorToken` and attributed to you, so it never appears under the review bot's identity. A project without that token cannot file findings from mrr at all.

`filePath` + `line` anchor it to the diff where the host accepts the position, and fall back to an unanchored thread where it does not.

post.description: Drops it before it ever reaches the forge. Deliberately not `WONT_FIX`: nothing was posted and nobody accepted a risk, so recording it as an accepted risk would put a claim on the record that nobody made.

post.description: The finding stays `OPEN` and keeps counting against the merge gate — a contested blocker that stops counting is how a ledger starts lying. What this records is the disagreement, on the finding's history, so it still ends in a real outcome: fixed, accepted, or won't fix.

post.description:
On a project with `holdFindings`, the reviewer stores its findings `PENDING` and posts nothing. This is what lets one through: it opens the thread, anchored to the line the reviewer named, and the finding becomes `OPEN`.

Posted under the review token, because it is still the reviewer's finding — releasing it says a person read it, not that they wrote it. Who released it is on the finding's history.

Send `title` or `body` to edit it on the way out; omit both to post it as written.

post.summary: Release a held finding onto the request

put.description:
`WONT_FIX` — real, and nobody is fixing it; you go on the record as having accepted the risk. `DUPLICATE` — another finding already covers it. `APPROVED` — accepted as it stands. `OPEN` — reopen it, which also clears the earlier sign-off.

`ADDRESSED` is not settable: it means a commit fixed the problem, which is the reviewer's verdict to reach, not a label to apply.

The thread on the request follows the state where the host can close and reopen threads.

post.description:
`identity` is an mrr user id, a forge username, or an agent role, according to `kind` — the same two identity spaces used everywhere else, with no mapping between them. Adding somebody already in the room updates their role rather than failing.

`required` is what makes a formal session more than a list of names: mrr will not call the request clean until every required participant signs off.

post.description:
Says **you** have looked at this merge request as it stands. You can only sign off as yourself: owning the project is not the same as being the person who was asked to review, and a sign-off somebody else recorded on your behalf would be the ledger claiming a review that never happened — which is the one thing a formal session exists to prevent.

That means only a `USER` participant can sign off here, matched against your own mrr user id. mrr has no way to authenticate a forge account, so a `FORGE` participant is a name on the list rather than someone who can press this; make them a `USER` participant if their sign-off has to gate the merge.

**A new commit clears every sign-off**, because approving what you read yesterday is not approving what was pushed since.

post.description:
Reviews the request as the forge has it right now, without waiting for a webhook or the catch-up scan. Works on a request mrr has never seen — it reads the merge request live rather than from anything already stored — so this is also how you get a cycle for one whose webhook was never registered.

Not a re-review. Reviews are keyed on `(project, mrIid, head sha)`, so asking twice on an unchanged commit returns `200` with the review that already exists and spends nothing. To force a fresh pass over the same commit, use `POST /api/reviews/{id}/rerun`.

Drafts are reviewed. `skipDrafts` exists so that every push to an unfinished branch does not cost a model call; asking for one explicitly answers that question.

200.description: A review of this commit already exists

put.description:
`AD_HOC` is the default and what every merge request has always had: the agent reviews, the status follows the findings, no ceremony. `FORMAL` adds the rule that mrr will not call the request `CLEAN` until every **required** participant has signed off, however few findings are left — and auto-approve follows the same rule, so mrr cannot approve a session its own status page calls `NEEDS_WORK`.

`sessionState` is where the *review* stands, which is not where the merge request stands: `CLOSED` here means the review is over, while merged and closed remain the forge's call and show in `currentStatus`.

get.description: Returns 200 once the HTTP listener is up and the context has started. It does not probe the database or GitLab — a green response means mrr is running, not that a review would succeed.

post.description:
Register this URL in the project's webhook settings with merge/pull request events ticked, using the secret returned when the project was created.

`{forge}` is `gitlab`, `forgejo` (also `gitea`, `codeberg`) or `github`, and must match the project's own forge. **`/webhooks/gitlab/{projectId}` keeps working forever** — every hook already registered in a GitLab UI points at it, and mrr does not create hooks.

Returns immediately. Fetching the diff and calling a model happen on a background worker, because hosts time deliveries out and retry them — blocking here would mean re-reviewing.

Only opened, reopened and updated actions are reviewed. Merge and close cancel any in-flight review and mark the cycle MERGED or CLOSED so the UI follows the host. Approvals are acknowledged and ignored.

Deduplicated on `(project, mr_iid, head sha)`. A redelivery, or an update that changed only a label, returns the existing review with `created: false` and spends nothing.
